script.title: Why Three-Quarters of French Troops Fell Sick

lines: A dying soldier's face turned blue-violet, and doctors called it the purple death.
France recorded influenza cases in April 1918.
Three-quarters of French troops fell sick during that first wave.
France had already lost nearly one point four million men killed or missing.
Another four million French soldiers were wounded.
Even so, French families kept sending their sons to the army.
The first wave disrupted French military operations.
Then a deadlier second wave arrived in autumn 1918.
Among hospitalized soldiers, the second wave's death rate was far higher.
October 1918 had the highest death rate of the whole pandemic.
World War I caused poor food, crowded camps, and bad hygiene.
Poor food and bad hygiene helped bacteria attack soldiers weakened by influenza.
Most victims died after a long death bed.
You see, a crowded hospital ward was like a packed bus: sickness had room to spread.
The real reason: influenza weakened soldiers, and bacteria caused a second infection.
Crowded camps and hospitals made that second infection deadly.
Here is the twist: soldiers who caught flu in spring were protected from death that fall.
Spring and summer exposure gave many soldiers protection against death.
The first wave was a disaster, and also a shield.

claims.claim: Further influenza cases were recorded in France in April 1918, and three-quarters of French troops fell sick during the first wave, which caused significant disruption to military operations.
Expiring patients developed a dusky heliotrope face and blue-violet cyanosis, which led to the name 'purple death'.
In the studied US Army camps and Britain, fatality among hospitalized soldiers was 1.1% in the first wave and 4.7% in the second wave.
October 1918 was the month with the highest fatality rate of the whole pandemic.
World War I exacerbated malnourishment, overcrowding in medical camps and hospitals, and poor hygiene, which promoted bacterial superinfection and killed most victims after a prolonged death bed.
France had nearly 1.4 million men killed or missing and another four million wounded, yet French families continued to send their sons into the army.
In the studied US Army camps and Britain, exposure to influenza in the spring and summer of 1918 provided 56 to 89 percent protection against death during the fall wave.
